about: CAT syllabus map (section -> topic -> subtopic) with concept notes written by ProCounsel. Topics follow the question bank's topic labels; 'match' lists lowercase keywords that map the bank's free-text subtopics onto a syllabus subtopic (see api/mba/syllabus.py). Notes are general maths/verbal concepts, not official exam facts.

subtopics.title: Main idea, purpose & structure
notes: The main idea is the one claim the whole passage supports. Test each option against every paragraph, not just the first or the last.
Options that are true but cover only one paragraph are too narrow; options that go beyond what the passage discusses are too broad.
For purpose questions, ask why the author wrote the passage: to argue, explain, compare, criticise or describe.
Map the passage as you read: one line per paragraph noting its job (claim, example, counter-view, conclusion).
A good summary keeps the author's stance and hedges ("may", "some", "often") intact.

subtopics.title: Inference & implication
notes: An inference must follow from the passage without outside knowledge: a small, safe step beyond what is stated.
Prefer cautious options. Extreme words (always, never, only, all) need explicit support in the text.
A faithful paraphrase of the passage is a valid answer to "which can be inferred".
Eliminate options that sound true in real life but are not supported by the passage.
"Consistent with the passage" means nothing in the text contradicts it; it need not be stated outright.

subtopics.title: Specific detail & EXCEPT questions
notes: Find the question's keyword in the passage and read two or three lines around it before choosing.
The right option usually paraphrases the text. An option that copies exact words but changes a relation (cause/effect, more/less) is a trap.
In EXCEPT/NOT questions three options are supported. Check each against the passage and pick the one that is not.
Mark the options you have already verified so you do not reread the passage again and again.

subtopics.title: Author's view & tone
notes: Separate the author's own opinion from views the author only reports ("critics argue", "some believe").
Tone words come in degrees (critical, sceptical, ambivalent, neutral, appreciative). Match the strength as well as the direction.
Evaluative words such as unfortunately, merely, rightly or overstated reveal the author's stance.
Academic passages are rarely extreme: options like "scathing" or "euphoric" are usually wrong unless the language is clearly that strong.

subtopics.title: Strengthen, weaken & assumptions
notes: First identify the conclusion and the evidence. A strengthener closes the gap between them; a weakener widens it.
An assumption is an unstated premise the argument needs. Negate the option: if the argument falls apart, it is the assumption.
Ignore options that are about the topic but not about the specific link in the argument.
A weakener need not disprove the conclusion; it only has to make it less likely.

subtopics.title: Function, examples & application
notes: For "the author mentions X in order to", find the claim X supports. Examples exist to illustrate, support or counter a point.
Application and analogy questions: reduce the passage's idea to an abstract pattern, then pick the option with the same pattern.
Ignore surface similarity (same subject matter) and match the logical structure instead.
"The author would most likely agree" questions stay within the passage's line of reasoning; do not extend it further than the author does.

subtopics.title: Vocabulary in context
notes: Words are tested in the sense the passage uses, which is often not the most common dictionary meaning.
Re-read the full sentence and substitute each option; the right one keeps the sentence's meaning and tone.
Use signal words (but, however, thus, similarly) to work out an unfamiliar word from its contrast or continuation.
Build vocabulary by reading editorials and long-form essays and noting new words with their sentences, not as isolated lists.

subtopics.title: Para jumbles
notes: Find a mandatory pair first: a sentence with a pronoun (this, they, such) or a connector (however, therefore) must follow the sentence it refers to.
The opening sentence introduces the topic and usually does not start with a pronoun or a connector.
Look for an order: chronology, general to specific, or problem → explanation → solution.
Once two or three links are fixed, build the sequence around them instead of testing every order.
When there are no options to check against, re-read your final sequence once as a paragraph.

subtopics.title: Para summary
notes: The best summary captures the paragraph's main point and its key qualification, and adds nothing new.
Eliminate options that focus on an example or a detail instead of the central idea.
Watch the scope: a summary broader or stronger than the paragraph is wrong.
Say the paragraph's point to yourself in one sentence before reading the options.

subtopics.title: Odd sentence out
notes: Four sentences form a coherent paragraph. The odd one is usually on the same broad topic but shifts focus, scope or viewpoint.
Build the paragraph from mandatory pairs first; the sentence that fits nowhere is the odd one.
Watch for a change of subject (a general idea to an unrelated specific case) or a change of time frame.
Do not drop a sentence only because its style differs; check whether it links logically.

subtopics.title: Sentence placement & completion
notes: Note what the sentence to be placed needs before it (a referent for "this" or "such") and what it leads into.
The correct slot makes the sentences on both sides connect smoothly.
Connectors in the sentence (however, as a result, for example) tell you its relation to the previous sentence.
For sentence completion, the ending must follow the paragraph's argument, not just its topic.

subtopics.title: Tables & missing data
notes: Before calculating, read the headings, units and totals; many questions need only one row or column.
For missing data, write each constraint (row totals, column totals, percentages) as an equation and fill the easiest cells first.
Track which values are exact and which are only ranges; some questions ask for the minimum or maximum possible value.
Approximate when the options are far apart; calculate exactly only when they are close.

subtopics.title: Bar, line, pie & other charts
notes: Check the scale and whether the axis starts at zero; bar heights can mislead.
Pie charts: a share of p% is 3.6 × p degrees. Convert to absolute numbers only when needed.
In a stacked bar, a segment's value is the difference between its top and bottom readings.
Scatter and bubble charts show two or three variables. Note what each axis and the bubble size stand for before answering.
Radar charts plot several measures on spokes; compare values along the same spoke only.

subtopics.title: Percentages, growth & averages in DI
notes: Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100; percentage share = part ÷ total × 100.
Growth over n periods at r% each: final = initial × (1 + r/100)ⁿ. When a question asks for the rate, compare growth rates, not absolute increases.
Weighted average = Σ(value × weight) ÷ Σ(weights); it always lies between the smallest and largest values.
The median of an ordered list is the middle value (the average of the two middle values for an even count).
Use fraction equivalents for fast approximation: 1/6 ≈ 16.67%, 1/7 ≈ 14.29%, 1/8 = 12.5%, 1/9 ≈ 11.11%.

subtopics.title: Networks, routes & schedules
notes: Draw the network: nodes for places or stages, arrows for flows, with the capacity or time on each edge.
Flow conservation: what enters a node equals what leaves it plus what stays there.
In a schedule or Gantt chart, a task starts only after the tasks it depends on finish; the longest chain of dependent tasks sets the minimum total time.
For minimum time or cost, list the routes systematically instead of trusting the shortest-looking one.

subtopics.title: Venn diagrams & set counting
notes: Two sets: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).
Three sets: n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) − n(A ∩ B) − n(B ∩ C) − n(C ∩ A) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C).
"Exactly two" and "at least two" are different regions: draw the diagram and fill the centre (all three) first.
For maximum or minimum questions, push the overlaps to the extreme the totals allow and check that every region stays non-negative.

subtopics.title: Arrangements (linear, circular, grid)
notes: Draw the structure first (a row of seats, a circle, a grid) and place the fixed clues before the relative ones.
In a circle, fix one person to remove rotations: n people can sit around a table in (n − 1)! distinct ways.
When everyone faces the centre, a person's left-hand neighbour is the next seat clockwise (seen from above).
If a clue allows two cases, draw both and let later clues eliminate one instead of guessing.
Keep a "cannot be here" list for each position; it often forces the last few placements.

subtopics.title: Scheduling, routes & processes
notes: Lay out a timeline grid (days × slots, or time × resources) and mark every fixed constraint first.
Process and flow sets follow rules step by step: simulate the first few steps carefully and look for a repeating pattern.
Queues: track arrival, waiting and service time in a table; service starts only when the previous item finishes.
Re-read conditions such as "before", "immediately before" and "not on consecutive days"; they are the usual traps.

subtopics.title: Distributions, grouping & relationships
notes: Make a table of people × attributes (or groups × items) and record ticks and crosses as you go.
Use totals: if each row or column must add up to a known value, the last unknown cell is forced.
For "at least one" and "at most two" conditions, list the extreme cases first.
Family-tree sets: draw generations as levels and record gender separately from relations.

subtopics.title: Tournaments, games & scoring
notes: Round robin with n teams: each team plays n − 1 matches, n(n − 1)/2 matches in all.
Knockout with n teams: n − 1 matches, because each match eliminates exactly one team.
The total points handed out across all matches follows from the scoring rule; use it to check your table.
For "minimum points to qualify", let the other teams take as many points as the rules allow and see what is left.
Write ratings and ranks as an inequality chain, and watch for ties.

subtopics.title: Venn-based reasoning
notes: The counting rules are the same as in DI Venn diagrams; the skill is turning sentences into regions.
"Only A" excludes everyone in B or C; "A and B" includes those also in C unless the clue says "only".
Name each unknown region with a variable and write one equation per given total.
Counts cannot be negative or fractional; these integer limits often pin down a unique answer.

subtopics.title: Number puzzles & optimisation
notes: Translate each condition into an equation or inequality; the unknowns are usually whole numbers.
For maximise/minimise questions, start from the extreme case and adjust until every condition holds.
Balance puzzles: each weighing has three outcomes, so k weighings can tell apart at most 3ᵏ cases.
Check your final answer against every clue; one missed condition is the most common error in these sets.

subtopics.title: Percentages
notes: x% of y = y% of x. Percentage change = change ÷ original × 100.
Successive changes of a% and b% give a net change of a + b + ab/100 per cent (use negative values for decreases).
If a price rises by r%, consumption must fall by r/(100 + r) × 100% to keep spending the same.
If A is r% more than B, then B is r/(100 + r) × 100% less than A.

subtopics.title: Profit, loss & discount
notes: Profit % and loss % are on the cost price; discount % is on the marked price.
SP = CP × (1 + profit%/100); SP = MP × (1 − discount%/100).
A mark-up of m% followed by a discount of d% gives a net profit of m − d − md/100 per cent.
Selling two items at the same price, one at x% profit and one at x% loss, always gives a net loss of x²/100 per cent.
False weights at cost price: profit % = (true weight − false weight) ÷ false weight × 100.

subtopics.title: Simple & compound interest
notes: SI = P × R × T ÷ 100; amount = P + SI.
CI amount = P(1 + R/100)ᵀ. Compounding k times a year: use rate R/k for kT periods.
CI − SI for 2 years = P(R/100)²; for 3 years = P(R/100)²(3 + R/100).
Equal instalments: bring each instalment back to today (divide by (1 + R/100)ⁿ) and set the total equal to the loan.
At R% compound interest money roughly doubles in 72/R years (the rule of 72 is an approximation).

subtopics.title: Ratio, proportion & mixtures
notes: If a : b = c : d then ad = bc. To combine a : b and b : c, make the common term equal first.
Alligation: mixing a cheaper item (price c) with a dearer one (price d) to get a mean price m needs the ratio (d − m) : (m − c).
Replacement: taking out x litres from V litres and refilling with water, n times, leaves V × (1 − x/V)ⁿ of the original liquid.
Partnership: profit is shared in the ratio of capital × time.
Direct variation y = kx; inverse variation y = k/x. Find k from one known pair.

subtopics.title: Averages & ages
notes: Average = sum ÷ count. Working with sums is usually faster than working with averages.
If one of n items changes by x, the average changes by x/n.
The combined average of two groups lies closer to the larger group's average.
Ages: the difference between two people's ages never changes, and everyone ages by the same amount.
The average of an arithmetic progression is (first term + last term) ÷ 2.

subtopics.title: Time & work, pipes & cisterns
notes: If A finishes a job in a days, A does 1/a of it per day; rates add when people work together.
Take the total work as the LCM of the individual times to avoid fractions.
Men × days × hours ÷ work is constant: M₁D₁H₁/W₁ = M₂D₂H₂/W₂.
Pipes: a filling pipe has a positive rate and an emptying pipe a negative rate.
Alternate-day work: find the work done in one full cycle, then handle the last partial cycle separately. Wages are shared in the ratio of work done.

subtopics.title: Time, speed & distance
notes: Distance = speed × time; km/h × 5/18 = m/s.
Average speed over two equal distances at speeds a and b is 2ab/(a + b), not (a + b)/2.
Relative speed: add the speeds when moving towards each other, subtract when moving in the same direction.
Trains: passing a pole covers the train's length; passing a platform or another train covers the sum of the lengths.
Boats: downstream = b + s, upstream = b − s, so boat speed = (down + up)/2 and stream speed = (down − up)/2.
Circular track, same direction, same start: the runners first meet after track length ÷ (difference of speeds).

subtopics.title: Word problems & linear equations
notes: Use one variable for the quantity asked and write everything else in terms of it.
n unknowns need n independent equations; with fewer, look for whole-number or range limits.
In MCQs, working back from the options is often fastest; start with a middle value.
Check the answer against the words of the question, not only against your equations.

subtopics.title: Linear & quadratic equations
notes: For ax² + bx + c = 0: sum of roots = −b/a, product = c/a, discriminant D = b² − 4ac.
D > 0: two distinct real roots; D = 0: equal roots; D < 0: no real roots.
With rational coefficients, irrational roots come in pairs p ± √q.
Identities: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²; a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b); a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²).
Remainder theorem: p(x) divided by (x − a) leaves the remainder p(a).

subtopics.title: Inequalities, modulus & maxima–minima
notes: Multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number reverses its sign.
|x − a| is the distance of x from a, so |x − a| < k means a − k < x < a + k.
AM ≥ GM for non-negative numbers: (a + b)/2 ≥ √(ab), with equality when a = b.
With a fixed product, a sum is smallest when the numbers are equal; with a fixed sum, a product is largest when they are equal.
Solve modulus equations by splitting at the points where each expression inside changes sign.

subtopics.title: Functions & graphs
notes: Domain: where the function is defined (no division by zero, no even root of a negative number, log only of a positive number).
f(g(x)) means apply g first, then f; f⁻¹ undoes f.
[x], the greatest integer function, is the largest integer ≤ x, so [−1.5] = −2.
Shifts: f(x) + k moves the graph up by k, f(x − k) moves it right by k, −f(x) reflects it in the x-axis, f(−x) in the y-axis.
Even functions: f(−x) = f(x). Odd functions: f(−x) = −f(x).

subtopics.title: Logarithms, exponents & surds
notes: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ, (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ, a⁰ = 1, a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ.
log(xy) = log x + log y; log(x/y) = log x − log y; log(xⁿ) = n log x.
Change of base: log_b a = log a ÷ log b, so log_b a × log_a b = 1.
logₐ x is defined only for x > 0, a > 0 and a ≠ 1; check every root you find against this.
Rationalise with the conjugate: 1/(√a + √b) = (√a − √b)/(a − b).

subtopics.title: Progressions & series
notes: AP: nth term = a + (n − 1)d; sum = n/2 × (2a + (n − 1)d) = n/2 × (first + last).
GP: nth term = arⁿ⁻¹; sum = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1); infinite sum = a/(1 − r) when |r| < 1.
1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2; sum of squares = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6; sum of cubes = [n(n + 1)/2]².
Take three numbers in AP as a − d, a, a + d and three in GP as a/r, a, ar.
For recurrences, write out the first few terms; a pattern or cycle usually appears quickly.

subtopics.title: Factors, divisibility, HCF & LCM
notes: If N = pᵃ × qᵇ × rᶜ (p, q, r prime), N has (a + 1)(b + 1)(c + 1) factors.
For two numbers, HCF × LCM = the product of the numbers.
Divisibility: by 3 or 9 if the digit sum is; by 8 if the last three digits are; by 11 if the difference between the sums of alternate digits is a multiple of 11.
Highest power of a prime p in n! = ⌊n/p⌋ + ⌊n/p²⌋ + ⌊n/p³⌋ + …
Trailing zeros of n! = the highest power of 5 in n!.

subtopics.title: Remainders & unit digits
notes: Remainders multiply and add: (a × b) mod n = (a mod n × b mod n) mod n.
Use negative remainders: 10 ≡ −1 (mod 11), so 10ᵏ leaves a remainder of (−1)ᵏ, i.e. 1 or 10.
Fermat: if p is prime and does not divide a, then a^(p − 1) leaves remainder 1 when divided by p.
Unit digits repeat in cycles of at most 4: 2 → 2, 4, 8, 6; 3 → 3, 9, 7, 1; 7 → 7, 9, 3, 1; 8 → 8, 4, 2, 6.
For two remainder conditions, list numbers that satisfy the larger divisor and test them against the other.

subtopics.title: Digits, bases & number forms
notes: A two-digit number with digits a and b is 10a + b; reversing it changes the value by 9(a − b).
In base b, (xyz)_b = x·b² + y·b + z, and every digit must be less than b.
Every palindrome with an even number of digits is divisible by 11.
Counting numbers by their digits is a permutation problem; remember the first digit cannot be 0.

subtopics.title: Integer solutions & parity
notes: ax + by = c has integer solutions only if g = HCF(a, b) divides c; from one solution, the others step by (b/g, −a/g).
x₁ + x₂ + … + x_k = n has C(n − 1, k − 1) positive-integer solutions and C(n + k − 1, k − 1) non-negative ones.
Parity: odd + odd = even and odd × odd = odd. Use it to rule out cases quickly.
Factorise expressions like xy + ax + by by adding ab: xy + ax + by + ab = (x + b)(y + a).

subtopics.title: Triangles
notes: Area = ½ × base × height = ½ab sin C. Heron's formula: √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)), with s the semi-perimeter.
Similar triangles with sides in ratio k have areas in ratio k².
The bisector of angle A divides BC in the ratio AB : AC.
Inradius r = area ÷ s; circumradius R = abc ÷ (4 × area).
Common Pythagorean triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25.
The medians meet at the centroid, which divides each median 2 : 1 from the vertex.

subtopics.title: Circles
notes: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc; the angle in a semicircle is 90°.
A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact; the two tangents from an outside point are equal.
In a cyclic quadrilateral, opposite angles add up to 180°.
Intersecting chords: AP × PB = CP × PD. Tangent and secant from P: PT² = PA × PB.
Sector area = (θ/360) × πr²; segment area = sector area − triangle area.

subtopics.title: Polygons & quadrilaterals
notes: Interior angles of an n-sided polygon add up to (n − 2) × 180°; each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 360°/n.
An n-sided polygon has n(n − 3)/2 diagonals.
Rhombus: the diagonals bisect each other at right angles; area = ½ × d₁ × d₂.
Trapezium area = ½ × (sum of the parallel sides) × height.
A regular hexagon of side a is six equilateral triangles: area = (3√3/2)a².

subtopics.title: Coordinate geometry
notes: Distance = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²); midpoint = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).
Slope m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have m₁ × m₂ = −1.
Distance from (x₁, y₁) to the line ax + by + c = 0 is |ax₁ + by₁ + c| ÷ √(a² + b²).
Triangle area from its vertices = ½|x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|.
Reflection of (x, y): in the x-axis (x, −y), in the y-axis (−x, y), in the line y = x (y, x).

subtopics.title: Mensuration (2D & 3D)
notes: Cylinder: volume πr²h, curved surface 2πrh.
Cone: volume ⅓πr²h, curved surface πrl, slant height l = √(r² + h²).
Sphere: volume (4/3)πr³, surface 4πr². Hemisphere: total surface 3πr².
Cuboid diagonal = √(l² + b² + h²). Cube of side a: volume a³, surface 6a².
Melting and recasting keeps the volume the same; cutting a solid increases its total surface area.

subtopics.title: Permutations & combinations
notes: nPr = n!/(n − r)! when order matters; nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!) when it does not.
Arrangements of n items with p alike, q alike, … = n!/(p! q! …).
n identical items into k distinct boxes (boxes may be empty): C(n + k − 1, k − 1) ways.
Use the complement: "at least one" = total − "none".
Choosing 2 of m horizontal lines and 2 of n vertical lines makes C(m, 2) × C(n, 2) rectangles.

subtopics.title: Probability
notes: P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total equally likely outcomes, so 0 ≤ P ≤ 1.
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
P(at least one) = 1 − P(none).
Two dice give 36 equally likely outcomes; a 6 × 6 grid makes sums easy to count.
Conditional probability: P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B).

subtopics.title: Set theory
notes: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B); extend it by inclusion–exclusion for three sets.
Numbers up to N divisible by a or b = ⌊N/a⌋ + ⌊N/b⌋ − ⌊N/LCM(a, b)⌋.
A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets.
For "maximum in none" or "minimum in all three", give each region a variable and use the totals.
